nameOfficial: Republic of Malawi (Republic of Malawi, Dziko la Malaŵi)
summary: The name "Malawi", readopted in 1964 from the Maravi kingdom, is said to have been chosen by Hastings Kamuzu Banda after he saw it on an eighteenth-century French map; the meaning of "flames" often attributed to it exists in Chichewa, but no scholarship establishes that the kingdom took its name from this. A British protectorate under the name Nyasaland until 1964, the country then readopted this older name. There, the Chewa, Tumbuka, Lomwe and Yao peoples continue the Gule Wamkulu, a great masked ritual.
etymology:
The name derives from that of the Maravi kingdom, which dominated the region during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and whose form circulated in Europe well before 1964: Livingstone reports in 1865 a "Lake Maravi" known from Portuguese sources, and d'Anville's map of Africa, published in Paris in 1749, carries a Lac Maravi. It was on a French map of this kind that Hastings Kamuzu Banda is said, according to his biographers, to have settled on his choice at independence, for the form and the sound of the word.

The meaning attributed to it is less certain. Jan Vermeullen's Chinyanja dictionary does give, under the root lawi, the form malawi for "flame of fire". But David Clement Scott's major Mang'anja dictionary, published in Edinburgh in 1892, does not know this root: it gives chirangali and kwiri for flame, and glosses "Malawi" as the Yao word meaning "tomorrow". No identified work links the name of the kingdom to this word, and the reference article on the beginnings of Maravi, published by Malyn Newitt in 1982, does not address the origin of the name. The explanation by the sun's reflections on the lake circulates widely; no source carrying this reading has been found.

The colonial name, for its part, illustrates a documented mechanism. Livingstone reports in 1865 that "nyanja or nyanza generally designates a marsh, a lake, a river, or even a simple stream", and recounts that his companions, asking to be led to the "Nyanja Mukulu", the great lake, were taken to a marsh that bore that name for their guide. The traveller asks for a proper name, and is answered with a common noun.
nameOriginActor: The name "Malawi" was made official at independence, in 1964, by the government of Hastings Kamuzu Banda, who took it from an old European map bearing a Lac Maravi. "Nyasaland" was the name of the British protectorate, formed on a word that Livingstone himself gives as a common noun denoting any body of water. Who named the Maravi kingdom, and on what basis, is not established.

historicalNames.antiquity: The present-day territory of Malawi was inhabited by various Bantu societies with no unified name. The indigenous peoples had their own names for their territories.
historicalNames.middleAges: Bantu migrations into the region. Development of local chiefdoms and kingdoms. No unified name for the territory as a whole.
historicalNames.precolonial: Sixteenth-seventeenth centuries: the Maravi kingdom, a powerful kingdom that dominated the region. The kingdom was centred on Lake Malawi (Lake Nyasa). Development of the Chewa, Tumbuka, Yao, Lomwe, Nyanja, Sena, Ngoni and Tonga chiefdoms. Regional trade and trade with the Portuguese. Europeans used the term "Nyasaland" (land of the Nyasa) to designate the region.
historicalNames.colonization: 1891-1964: British protectorate of Nyasaland (Nyasaland Protectorate). The British established a protectorate over Nyasaland in 1891. The territory was administered as a British protectorate until independence in 1964.
historicalNames.contemporary: 1964: independence of Nyasaland (6 July 1964), proclamation of the Republic of Malawi. The name "Malawi" was made official at independence to replace "Nyasaland".

kingdoms.name: Maravi Kingdom
kingdoms.historicalRole: A powerful Maravi kingdom, matrilineal system, development of regional trade, relations with the Portuguese. The kingdom was centred on Lake Malawi (Lake Nyasa). Founded by the Chewa.

kingdoms.name: Chewa chiefdoms
kingdoms.historicalRole: Chewa chiefdoms, matrilineal system, cultural traditions (Gule Wamkulu masks, a major initiation ritual), agriculture (maize). Heirs of the Maravi kingdom.

kingdoms.name: Tumbuka chiefdoms
kingdoms.historicalRole: Tumbuka chiefdoms, cultural traditions, patrilineal lineage structures.

kingdoms.name: Yao chiefdoms
kingdoms.historicalRole: Yao chiefdoms, Islamic traditions, regional trade, resistance to British colonisation.

kingdoms.name: British Protectorate of Nyasaland
dominantPeoples: Tous les peuples malawiens sous protectorat britannique
kingdoms.historicalRole: British protectorate, development of colonial administration, resistance from indigenous peoples (notably Yao resistance). Development of the independence movement in the twentieth century, leadership of Hastings Kamuzu Banda.

culture.culturalTraditions: Significant cultural diversity reflecting Malawi's ethnic mosaic. Bantu traditions: Gule Wamkulu masks (Chewa, a major initiation ritual), traditional music, traditional dance. Matrilineal traditions (Chewa, matrilineal system). Patrilineal traditions (Tumbuka, other peoples). Islamic traditions (Yao). Varied traditional music and dance. Rites of passage, initiation rites, traditional festivals. Lake Malawi (Lake Nyasa) is a central element of Malawian culture and economy.
culture.dominantReligions: Christianity (majority Protestantism, Catholicism, African independent churches), Islam (minority, Yao), traditional African religions (frequent syncretism, ancestor worship, masks, rituals)
culture.lifestyles: Agriculture (maize, tobacco, tea, food crops), fishing (Lake Malawi, an important source of protein), livestock farming (cattle, goats), trade and urban activities (urban areas, Lilongwe, Blantyre). Moderate urbanisation. An economy based on agriculture (maize, tobacco and tea, the main exports), fishing, and services. Malawi is one of the poorest countries in Africa.
culture.socialOrganization: Organisation into historical kingdoms (the Maravi kingdom), traditional chiefdoms (Chewa, Tumbuka, Yao, Lomwe, Nyanja, Sena, Ngoni, Tonga), matrilineal (Chewa) and patrilineal (Tumbuka, other peoples) clan structures. The importance of lineages and extended families. The role of councils of elders. Initiation traditions and rites of passage to adulthood. Matrilineal system (Chewa).
culture.regionalRelations: Historical relations with Mozambique (trade, migrations, cross-border peoples, the border), Zambia (Tumbuka, trade, the border), Tanzania (trade, the border). Integration into the SADC (Southern African Development Community). Cross-border trade and cultural relations. Lake Malawi is shared with Mozambique and Tanzania.

historicalFacts.ancientPeriods: Initial settlement by Bantu peoples. Bantu migrations into the region. Development of local chiefdoms.
historicalFacts.middleAges: Continued Bantu migrations. Development of local political structures. Contacts with neighbouring peoples.
historicalFacts.precolonial: Sixteenth-seventeenth centuries: the Maravi kingdom, a powerful kingdom that dominated the region, centred on Lake Malawi. Consolidation of the Chewa, Tumbuka, Yao, Lomwe, Nyanja, Sena, Ngoni and Tonga chiefdoms. Regional trade and trade with the Portuguese. Nineteenth century: Ngoni migrations (Zulu migrants). Development of cultural traditions.
historicalFacts.colonization: 1891: establishment of the British protectorate of Nyasaland. British colonial period (1891-1964), development of colonial administration, resistance from indigenous peoples (notably Yao resistance). Twentieth century: development of the independence movement, leadership of Hastings Kamuzu Banda.
historicalFacts.independenceStruggle: 1950s-1964: independence movement led by Hastings Kamuzu Banda and the Malawi Congress Party (MCP). 1964: independence of Nyasaland (6 July 1964), proclamation of the Republic of Malawi. Hastings Kamuzu Banda becomes the first president.
historicalFacts.postIndependence: 1964-1994: presidency of Hastings Kamuzu Banda, an authoritarian regime, a one-party state. 1994-present: democratic transition, multi-party elections, the presidencies of Bakili Muluzi (1994-2004), Bingu wa Mutharika (2004-2012), Joyce Banda (2012-2014), Peter Mutharika (2014-2020), and Lazarus Chakwera (since 2020). Challenges: poverty, economic development, HIV/AIDS, food security. Malawi is one of the poorest countries in Africa.
